strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored systems problem in cooperative V2X perception: reducing model inference, memory, and communication costs jointly rather than optimizing perception accuracy alone. This is well aligned with an Applied/Systems contribution, which seems more appropriate than a purely Algorithms/General framing.

The proposed full-stack quantization recipe is practically motivated and reasonably comprehensive: it combines model PTQ, fusion-stage alignment losses, and codebook-index transmission to attack local inference, fusion inference, and communication payload together.

Experiments cover several relevant cooperative perception datasets and settings, including DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V, and evaluate multiple fusion architectures. The reported results show small accuracy drops for Pyramid Fusion under INT4/INT8 model-level quantization and substantial system-level latency reduction.

The paper includes useful ablations on alignment losses, calibration set size, calibration steps, PTQ baselines, codebook size/repetition, and power/throughput. These strengthen the practical case and make the empirical story broader than a single benchmark number.

The work is clearly motivated and mostly readable, with a valuable emphasis on deployment-oriented metrics such as latency, communication size, memory constraints, and energy/query rather than only idealized AP/mAP.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. Much of the method combines established ingredients: max-min/PTQ calibration, AdaRound-style learnable rounding, block reconstruction, KL/L2 alignment, and codebook-based feature communication. The paper would be stronger if it more sharply isolated what is technically new beyond adapting and integrating these components for V2X.

Some technical formulations appear incorrect or imprecise. The quantization scale equation is written as a function of qmax and qmin rather than the floating-point tensor range, and the communication-bandwidth expressions take log2 of an already size-like product, which is dimensionally confusing. These issues do not necessarily invalidate the implementation, but they weaken technical rigor and reproducibility.

The strongest claims about real-world deployment are somewhat overstated. Latency is measured with TensorRT/custom CUDA on RTX 3090 and averaged over only 10 runs, while system-level perception performance is evaluated using a latency/asynchrony simulation formula. This is useful evidence, but not the same as comprehensive C-V2X or in-vehicle edge deployment under real network conditions.

The system-level mAP gains over full precision are partly a consequence of the latency/asynchrony evaluation setup, not because the quantized model is intrinsically more accurate. The paper should make this distinction clearer and provide more sensitivity analyses over bandwidth, delay distributions, number of agents, and hardware platforms.

The baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. CodeFilling and Where2comm are compared, but it is unclear whether all baselines receive equally optimized TensorRT/custom-kernel deployment and equally tuned compression/latency treatment. A quantized CodeFilling or codebook-only plus PTQ decomposition would better attribute the gains.

Generalizability is mixed: V2X-ViT suffers severe degradation under quantization, especially at 4/8 bits, which undercuts the claim that the approach generalizes across fusion methods. The limitation is acknowledged, but the main text still presents broad generality more strongly than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility depends on promised code release and custom CUDA/TensorRT plugins. Important implementation details such as exact kernel behavior, calibration sampling, model export constraints, and hardware-specific measurement protocol are not sufficiently specified for independent replication from the paper alone.

The paper lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated-trial variance for accuracy and latency, which matters because some reported gains over strong communication-efficient baselines are modest, for example the 1.2 mAP30 improvement over CodeFilling in the system-level table.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: reducing inference, communication, and memory costs for V2X cooperative perception. This deployment-oriented framing is valuable for ECCV, especially because many cooperative perception papers report idealized accuracy without system latency.

The experiments cover several relevant datasets and fusion models, including DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V, and include model-level accuracy, latency breakdowns, calibration ablations, and comparisons to some PTQ and communication-efficient baselines.

The best reported results suggest that low-bit model quantization plus codebook-based communication can preserve much of the full-precision detection accuracy while substantially reducing measured latency, which is a useful empirical observation for this community.

The paper acknowledges an important limitation: some architectures, especially V2X-ViT, degrade severely under aggressive quantization, indicating that quantization-aware cooperative architectures may be needed.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited. The method appears to combine existing ingredients: max-min/PTQ calibration, AdaRound-style learnable rounding, block reconstruction, distillation/alignment losses, and codebook-based feature transmission closely related to CodeFilling. The claimed “first fully quantized” system is more of an engineering integration than a clearly new algorithmic contribution, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish its technical contribution from prior quantization and codebook communication methods.

The system-level evidence is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. Latency is measured partly on RTX 3090/A6000-class GPUs rather than clearly resource-constrained automotive hardware, while the paper repeatedly frames the method as real-world edge deployment. The “real-world testing platform” details are mostly illustrative and lack enough specificity to validate deployment realism.

The communication-latency modeling is questionable and under-specified. The formula and units are unclear, and the reported transmission sizes/latencies do not appear easy to reconcile with a 27 Mbps link. The added uniform asynchronous delay is also not clearly justified or separated in the analysis, making the reported system-level mAP improvements difficult to interpret.

The comparison protocol is potentially unfair or muddled. The full-precision baselines transmit BEV features with different compression settings, while QuantV2X uses a codebook representation; it is therefore unclear how much of the gain comes from model quantization versus adopting an existing communication-efficient representation. The improvement over CodeFilling is relatively small, yet the paper frames the overall system gain as much larger.

The paper’s technical description has inconsistencies. It calls the method post-training quantization, but the pipeline includes codebook pretraining and joint optimization of the encoder, fusion module, detection head, and codebook. This blurs the distinction between PTQ and retraining/fine-tuning, and the exact supervision, calibration data usage, and optimization variables are not described with enough rigor for reproducibility.

Some equations and definitions appear incorrect or imprecise. For example, the communication bandwidth expressions use logarithms of byte counts in a way that does not correspond to actual payload size, and the quantization scale formula is written as (qmax - qmin)/(2^b - 1), omitting the data range that should determine the scale. These issues weaken confidence in the technical soundness.

The ablation evidence is thin. The alignment module’s contribution is shown mostly as small AP gains over an already strong baseline for selected settings, and there is no sufficiently clean decomposition of model quantization, activation calibration, codebook messaging, spatial alignment, heterogeneity alignment, and latency compensation across datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details about custom CUDA/TensorRT plugins, exact model architectures, calibration sampling, compression modules, hardware settings, and the promised public release are insufficient; the abstract even leaves the release link blank.

The writing repeatedly overclaims practical deployment and real-world viability relative to the evidence. The results are interesting, but they do not establish that the system is deployable in safety-critical V2X conditions, robust to real communication stacks, or validated on representative automotive edge devices.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical bottleneck in V2X cooperative perception: deployment efficiency rather than only idealized perception accuracy. Treating this as an Applied/Systems contribution is appropriate, and the system-level framing is valuable for ECCV because latency, bandwidth, and memory are central to real cooperative perception deployment.

QuantV2X is a coherent full-stack design that combines end-to-end model quantization with quantized/codebook-based feature transmission. The work makes a convincing case that communication and inference should be optimized jointly rather than separately.

The experimental coverage is broad: results are reported on DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V; across several fusion methods; and under both model-level and system-level settings. The reported preservation of accuracy under INT4/INT8 and the 3.2x latency reduction are strong empirical signals.

The paper includes useful ablations on alignment losses, calibration set size, calibration steps, codebook configuration, and comparisons with PTQ baselines. These help isolate the main components and support the claim that the alignment module matters in heterogeneous multi-agent settings.

The emphasis on reproducibility and deployability is positive: the paper states that the system will be released, builds on existing HEAL/V2X-ReaLO infrastructure, and discusses TensorRT/CUDA deployment considerations rather than remaining purely algorithmic.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level. The PTQ procedure draws heavily on known calibration, block reconstruction, and AdaRound-style ideas, while the codebook communication resembles prior CodeFilling/codebook approaches. The contribution is strongest as an integrated system, but the paper could be clearer about which parts are fundamentally new versus adapted.

The system-level evaluation is promising but not fully conclusive. Latency is measured mainly on RTX 3090-class hardware and averaged over only 10 runs, while the paper’s motivation concerns in-vehicle, resource-constrained platforms. More extensive profiling on automotive/edge hardware, with variance and worst-case latency, would strengthen the deployment claim.

Some details in the latency and communication modeling are unclear or potentially inconsistent. The communication-size formulas appear dimensionally odd, and the relation between measured latency, simulated delay, feature size, and transmission rate is not fully transparent. Since the paper’s main claim depends on system-level latency, this needs sharper exposition.

The method shows serious degradation for at least one important attention-based architecture, V2X-ViT, especially under low-bit quantization. The limitation is acknowledged, but it weakens the claim of broad generality across cooperative perception models.

The real-world robustness evaluation is still limited. The paper considers pose errors and latency, but does not deeply evaluate packet loss, bandwidth fluctuations, synchronization failures, multi-agent scaling beyond the reported settings, or safety-critical failure modes.

Implementation details for the custom TensorRT plugins/CUDA kernels, exact quantization coverage for difficult operations, and codebook training/reconstruction are not sufficient to fully assess reproducibility before release. More precise engineering details would make the contribution easier to validate independently.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic one: its main value is a full-stack quantized V2X cooperative perception pipeline that jointly targets model inference, message transmission, memory footprint, and deployment latency. Under that lens, the problem is important and timely for real-world cooperative perception.

The empirical scope is broad. The manuscript evaluates on DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V, and V2X-ReaLO, considers multiple fusion families, reports model-level AP, system-level latency/accuracy, robustness to pose noise, calibration-set/step ablations, codebook-size ablations, power/throughput, and some online ROS-based results.

The main systems result is compelling: quantization plus codebook messages substantially reduces measured latency and bandwidth, and in latency-aware settings QuantV2X approaches the ideal full-precision upper bound while outperforming online full-precision baselines. This supports the paper's central argument that lower numerical precision can improve deployed perception by improving timeliness.

The paper includes useful component analyses. The alignment losses improve over max-min/AdaRound baselines, especially for AP50/AP70 and long-range detections, and the decomposition of model-side versus communication-side optimization helps justify why both are needed.

The work appears practically oriented, with TensorRT/ONNX deployment, custom kernels for unsupported quantized modules, and an intention to release the system. This kind of deployment evidence is valuable for ECCV when the contribution is framed as systems work.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. Much of the method combines known ingredients: min-max calibration, AdaRound-style rounding, block reconstruction, feature/codebook compression related to CodeFilling, and distillation-style alignment losses. The paper would benefit from a sharper explanation of what is technically new beyond adapting these components to V2X.

Several technical descriptions are imprecise or possibly incorrect. The communication-volume formulas apply log2 to the whole byte count rather than computing bits/bytes directly, Eq. 6 defines the quantization scale in terms of qmax/qmin rather than the observed tensor range, and the text reverses the min/max calibration interval as [Xmax, Xmin]. These may be writing errors, but they weaken confidence in the rigor of the presentation.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for a deployment-heavy paper. It is unclear exactly which layers/operators remain full precision, whether quantization is per-channel or per-tensor, how activation observers are implemented, how zero-points are optimized, what calibration samples/agent combinations are used, and how the custom TensorRT plugins affect latency and portability.

The system-level evaluation mixes measured and simulated quantities in a way that is not fully disentangled. Main V2X-Real performance uses a latency model with a fixed 27 Mbps rate and U(0,200 ms) delay, while latency is averaged over only 10 runs on an RTX 3090 rather than typical automotive hardware. The V2X-ReaLO online results help, but they are limited and lack variance, statistical analysis, and comparisons to all communication-efficient baselines.

Some headline claims are overstated. The reported +9.5 mAP30 gain is relative to a latency-degraded full-precision baseline with no compression, while the ideal full-precision upper bound remains slightly higher. Thus QuantV2X is not intrinsically more accurate than full precision; it is more effective under the chosen latency/deployment model.

Generalization is mixed. The method works well for Pyramid Fusion, but V2X-ViT suffers severe degradation under INT4/8, and the system-level experiments focus mainly on PointPillar/Pyramid Fusion. This limits the strength of the claim that the recipe broadly supports heterogeneous cooperative perception models.

The memory-scaling claim is under-supported. Fig. 7 is qualitative and lacks enough numeric detail about model sizes, GPU budgets, memory accounting, and selected backbones to substantiate the assertion that QuantV2X enables larger models under strict resource budgets.

Baseline coverage could be stronger. The PTQ comparison is mainly against PD-Quant and LiDAR-PTQ on one DAIR-V2X setting, with limited comparison to stronger or more recent quantization recipes, QAT alternatives, mixed precision, or hardware-aware quantization. The FP16 comparison is also a weak proxy for low-precision deployment baselines.

strengths: The paper addresses an important applied/systems problem: cooperative V2X perception is often evaluated in idealized full-precision settings, while real deployment depends on latency, bandwidth, memory, and edge inference efficiency. This is a worthwhile direction for ECCV.

The manuscript evaluates multiple aspects of the system, including model-level quantization, communication payload, latency decomposition, memory-budget scaling, power consumption, and several datasets/fusion methods. This broader evaluation is more deployment-aware than a purely AP-focused paper.

The empirical results suggest that INT8/INT4 quantization with the proposed calibration/alignment losses can largely preserve AP for some cooperative perception pipelines, and the reported system-level numbers indicate clear efficiency gains over unoptimized full-precision baselines.

The paper is generally readable and makes a concrete attempt to integrate model quantization and communication compression into a unified V2X pipeline rather than treating them as separate optimizations.
weaknesses: I assess this primarily as an Applied/Systems paper. Under that standard, the central weakness is that the evidence for a deployable full system is not sufficiently rigorous. The main system-level performance table appears to combine measured model latency with simulated communication/asynchrony assumptions, while the real-world V2X-ReaLO evidence is relegated to the appendix and lacks enough implementation detail, variance, and controlled ablations to substantiate the strongest deployment claims.

The technical novelty is limited. The method largely combines existing ingredients: PTQ/block reconstruction, AdaRound-style rounding, codebook-based communication, and feature/output alignment losses. The paper claims a first fully quantized V2X system, but the algorithmic contribution beyond adapting known tools to this setting is modest and not sharply separated from prior work such as LiDAR-PTQ and CodeFilling.

Several methodological details are underspecified or internally unclear. The codebook communication formulation gives bandwidth expressions using log2 of a byte count, which is dimensionally wrong for communication volume. The description of multiple codes, product quantization, Gumbel-Softmax weights, and reconstruction does not fully specify what is transmitted and reconstructed at inference. The alignment module is described as losses during calibration rather than a clearly defined module, despite being central to the claimed contribution.

The comparisons are not fully convincing. CodeFilling is the closest communication baseline, LiDAR-PTQ/PD-Quant are the closest PTQ baselines, but the paper does not provide a clean full-system comparison against combinations of strong existing quantization plus strong existing communication compression. This makes it hard to attribute gains to the proposed design rather than to the fact that baselines optimize only one part of the pipeline.

The reported improvement over full precision can be misleading. The upper-bound full-precision model has better ideal accuracy, while QuantV2X wins only after latency/asynchrony penalties are introduced. This is a legitimate systems argument, but the paper sometimes phrases the result as broadly surpassing full precision without making the dependence on the latency model sufficiently explicit.

Experimental reporting lacks important reproducibility and statistical detail. Latency is averaged over only 10 runs on RTX 3090, calibration uses 5000 steps and custom TensorRT/CUDA plugins without sufficient description, and no confidence intervals or sensitivity to bandwidth/asynchrony assumptions are provided. For a systems-oriented claim, these omissions are significant.

The scaling-under-memory experiment is visually presented but not quantified enough to evaluate. The exact memory budgets, selected backbones, model sizes, and AP values are not clearly tabulated, weakening one of the paper's main claims about enabling larger models under edge GPU constraints.

The paper overclaims in places. Phrases such as “fully quantized,” “real-world deployment,” and “first fully quantized multi-agent system” are stronger than what is demonstrated, especially given that some components reconstruct features locally and the deployment evaluation is only partially real-world and not deeply characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored deployment problem in V2X cooperative perception: reducing end-to-end latency, communication bandwidth, and memory pressure rather than optimizing only offline AP. This is a timely and practically relevant framing for ECCV.

QuantV2X is evaluated as a full system, combining model-side PTQ with communication-side codebook index transmission. The reported reductions are substantial: about 3.2x lower system latency and system-level mAP much closer to the ideal upper bound on V2X-Real than full-precision online baselines.

The experimental coverage is broad: DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V, multiple fusion architectures, heterogeneous camera/LiDAR settings, pose-noise robustness, calibration-size/step ablations, comparisons to PD-Quant and LiDAR-PTQ, power measurements, and additional V2X-ReaLO online results.

The component analyses support the main technical choices. The alignment losses improve INT4/INT8 recovery, especially under heterogeneous settings and stricter/long-range metrics, and the decomposition of computation vs communication latency helps justify the full-stack design.

The work has clear potential impact for deployable cooperative perception. Even if individual ingredients build on known PTQ, AdaRound-style rounding, and codebook compression, their integration and evaluation in a multi-agent V2X system is valuable.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. Much of the method combines established ingredients: block-wise PTQ, AdaRound-inspired rounding, codebook-based feature compression, and feature/output distillation-style alignment. The paper’s strongest contribution is systems integration and evaluation, not a fundamentally new quantization method.

Some technical details are underspecified for reproducibility, including exact quantization granularity, treatment of difficult operators, hyperparameters for scale search and alignment losses, CUDA/TensorRT plugin details, calibration sampling protocol, and whether all reported calibration is strictly label-free as expected for PTQ.

The system-level evaluation is convincing in direction but still partly simulation-driven. The main V2X-Real results use a prescribed communication delay model and only the appendix reports online V2X-ReaLO deployment. More details on edge hardware, wireless conditions, synchronization, variance over runs, and failure cases would make the real-world claims stronger.

The latency measurements are averaged over only 10 runs on an RTX 3090, which is not representative of many automotive edge platforms. The paper argues for in-vehicle deployment, so results on actual embedded accelerators or automotive-grade hardware would better support the deployment claims.

There are a few presentation and formulation issues. For example, the communication bandwidth formulas appear to use a logarithm over the whole payload size, which is dimensionally confusing or likely incorrect. Several sections read as response-to-review style Q&A rather than polished paper text, and some key claims such as '+9.5 mAP30 over full precision' need careful contextualization because they are under latency constraints rather than ideal accuracy.

Comparisons to prior communication-efficient methods are useful but not exhaustive. The paper would benefit from stronger apples-to-apples comparisons against more recent cooperative perception compression/selection methods and from reporting variance or confidence intervals, since small AP differences separate QuantV2X from CodeFilling in some settings.
